\chapter{Until When}
\label{ch:until-when}
\hlchaptermodality{13}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can pick the farewell that matches when I will next see someone.}

Until When — the chapter run end to end.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hasta luego]{hasta luego — the everyday \textquotedblleft{}see you later\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C05-hasta-luego}



\begin{quote}
This is the goodbye you'll actually use most — friendly, casual, open-ended. \textbf{hasta luego}: \textquotedblleft{}until later.\textquotedblright{} You already own \textbf{hasta} (\textquotedblleft{}until\textquotedblright{}); today you add \textbf{luego} (\textquotedblleft{}later\textquotedblright{}), and it has a very Latin backstory.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ue} — \textbf{luego} = \emph{LWEH-goh}: the \emph{ue} is a \emph{w}-glide, \emph{lweh-}.
  \item The whole phrase: \emph{AHS-tah LWEH-goh}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{hasta luego} = \textquotedblleft{}until later\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you later.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hasta} = \textquotedblleft{}until\textquotedblright{} (last lesson — Arabic \emph{ḥattā}).
  \item \textbf{luego} = \textquotedblleft{}later / then / soon,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{loco}, \textquotedblleft{}at the place / at that point.\textquotedblright{} The idea slid from \emph{place} $\to$ \emph{point in time} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}then, next, soon.\textquotedblright{} So its cousins in English are all about \textbf{place}: \textbf{local}, \textbf{locus}, \textbf{loc}ation, \textbf{loc}ate, \textbf{al-loc-ate}. Spanish moved \emph{loco} from \emph{where} to \emph{when}.
\end{itemize}

A nice contrast: \textbf{hasta luego} fuses an \textbf{Arabic} word and a \textbf{Latin} word in three syllables — the two great layers of Spanish, shaking hands as you leave.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the \textquotedblleft{}hasta …\textquotedblright{} family}]
\emph{hasta} + a time word is Spanish's whole toolkit of soft goodbyes. You'll build the other two this chapter:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{phrase} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}until …\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{when} \\
\midrule
\textbf{hasta luego} & later & the default \textquotedblleft{}see you\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{hasta mañana} & tomorrow & leaving for the day \\
\textbf{hasta pronto} & soon & you expect to meet again shortly \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hasta luego\textquotedblright{} — \emph{AHS-tah LWEH-goh}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}luego\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}local, location\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{loco} \textquotedblleft{}place\textquotedblright{} family
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¡Adiós! … no — ¡hasta luego!\textquotedblright{} — feel the difference: final vs. soon
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{hasta luego} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Until later.\textquotedblright{}) What did \emph{luego}'s Latin root \emph{loco} first mean, and what English words keep it? (Place — \emph{local, location, locus}.) Which two language layers meet in \emph{hasta luego}? (Arabic \emph{hasta} + Latin \emph{luego}.) Next: \textbf{hasta mañana}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hasta mañana]{hasta mañana — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} (and the ñ returns)}

\label{lesson:ES-C05-hasta-manana}



\begin{quote}
Leaving for the day? \textbf{hasta mañana} — \textquotedblleft{}until tomorrow.\textquotedblright{} It brings back a letter you studied in the writing lessons: the \textbf{ñ}. Here it is, living in a word you'll say every evening.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{enye-ny} — \textbf{mañana} = \emph{mah-NYAH-nah}: the \textbf{ñ} is the squished \emph{ny} of \textquotedblleft{}canyon\textquotedblright{} (your ñ writing lesson — the tilde is a tiny second \emph{n}, remember). Three soft \emph{ah}'s: \emph{ma-\textbf{ÑA}-na}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{hasta mañana} = \textquotedblleft{}until tomorrow\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hasta} = \textquotedblleft{}until\textquotedblright{} (Arabic \emph{ḥattā}).
  \item \textbf{mañana} = \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{and} \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{} One word for both, from Latin \textbf{(hōra) maneana}, \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{early} hour\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{māne}, \textquotedblleft{}in the morning\textquotedblright{}). The logic: the next \textquotedblleft{}early hour\textquotedblright{} you'll see is \emph{tomorrow morning} $\to$ \emph{mañana} came to mean both \textbf{morning} and \textbf{tomorrow}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The ñ, in the wild.} Recall the writing lesson: \emph{ñ} is a frozen \emph{nn} — a scribe's shorthand for a doubled \emph{n}. \emph{mañana} comes from Latin \emph{maneana}, whose \emph{n}+\emph{ea} palatalized (softened) into that single \emph{ñ} sound. So the tilde is a little historical fossil sitting in the middle of \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: same word, two meanings — context decides}]
\emph{mañana} means \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} \textbf{or} \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}; the sentence tells you which. Paired with \emph{hasta}, it's always \textbf{tomorrow}: \emph{hasta mañana}, \textquotedblleft{}until tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mañana\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mah-NYAH-nah}, squished \emph{ñ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hasta mañana\textquotedblright{} — until tomorrow
  \item “mañana” once as “morning,” then once as “tomorrow” — context decides
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two meanings does \emph{mañana} carry? (Morning; tomorrow.) With \emph{hasta}, which one? (Tomorrow.) What sound is the \emph{ñ}, and what is its tilde, historically? (The \emph{ny} of \textquotedblleft{}canyon\textquotedblright{}; a frozen doubled-\emph{n}.) Next: \textbf{hasta pronto}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hasta pronto]{hasta pronto — \textquotedblleft{}see you soon\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C05-hasta-pronto}



\begin{quote}
The last of the \textquotedblleft{}hasta …\textquotedblright{} trio: \textbf{hasta pronto}, \textquotedblleft{}until soon\textquotedblright{} — for when you genuinely expect to meet again shortly. One new word, \textbf{pronto}, and it's hiding in plain sight in English.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hasta pronto} = \emph{AHS-tah PRON-toh} — a clean \emph{pr}, a pure \emph{o}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{hasta pronto} = \textquotedblleft{}until soon\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you soon.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hasta} = \textquotedblleft{}until\textquotedblright{} (Arabic \emph{ḥattā}).
  \item \textbf{pronto} = \textquotedblleft{}soon / quickly / ready,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{promptus}, \textquotedblleft{}brought forth, ready at hand\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{prōmere}, \textquotedblleft{}to bring out\textquotedblright{}). Something \emph{prompt} is brought out \textbf{without delay} — so \emph{pronto} slid to \textquotedblleft{}soon.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

You already know its English twin: \textbf{prompt} (on time; to bring out a response), plus \textbf{prompt}er, \textbf{prompt}ly, and the computer \textbf{prompt} (the cursor \textquotedblleft{}ready\textquotedblright{} for input). Italian borrowed \emph{pronto} too — it's what Italians say when they pick up the phone (\emph{\textquotedblleft{}Pronto!\textquotedblright{}} = \textquotedblleft{}Ready!\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the \textquotedblleft{}hasta …\textquotedblright{} trio, complete}]
You now have Spanish's three soft goodbyes, sharpest to vaguest in time:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{phrase} & \textbf{until…} & \textbf{nuance} \\
\midrule
\textbf{hasta pronto} & soon & you'll meet again shortly \\
\textbf{hasta luego} & later & the neutral default \textquotedblleft{}see you\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{hasta mañana} & tomorrow & you're parting for the day \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

…and \textbf{adiós} for the long or final goodbye.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \textquotedblleft{}hasta pronto\textquotedblright{} — \emph{AHS-tah PRON-toh}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pronto\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}prompt, promptly\textquotedblright{} — one family
  \item the trio — hasta pronto / hasta luego / hasta mañana
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{hasta pronto} mean, and \emph{pronto}'s English twin? (\textquotedblleft{}Until soon\textquotedblright{}; \emph{prompt}.) What Latin word is it from, and its literal sense? \section[Practice]{Practice — saying goodbye}

\label{lesson:ES-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. This chapter's farewells — \emph{adiós} and the three \emph{hasta …} goodbyes — now close a real conversation, and fold back into the whole arc you've built since \emph{hola}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: choosing the right goodbye}]
The choice is about \textbf{when you'll meet again}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you're…} & \textbf{say} \\
\midrule
parting for good / a long time & \textbf{Adiós.} \\
expecting to meet again shortly & \textbf{Hasta pronto.} \\
just \textquotedblleft{}see you\textquotedblright{} (neutral default) & \textbf{Hasta luego.} \\
leaving for the day & \textbf{Hasta mañana.} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange — start to finish}
Everything from Chapters 1–5, in one conversation:

\begin{quote}
— ¡Hola! Buenos días. Me llamo Ana. ¿Cómo se llama usted? — Me llamo Luis. Mucho gusto. — ¿Cómo está usted? — Bien, gracias. ¿Y usted? — Bien. \textbf{Hasta mañana}, Luis. — \textbf{Hasta mañana}, Ana. \textbf{¡Adiós!}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{adiós} — the plain/final goodbye (\textquotedblleft{}to God\textquotedblright{}; twin of \emph{goodbye}).
  \item \textbf{hasta} — \textquotedblleft{}until,\textquotedblright{} Spain's everyday Arabic word ($\leftarrow$ \emph{ḥattā}).
  \item \textbf{hasta luego / mañana / pronto} — see you later / tomorrow / soon, each an Arabic + Latin handshake.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the full conversation above, both voices — greeting to goodbye
  \item pick the goodbye — for a friend you'll see tomorrow? (hasta mañana); for someone moving away? (adiós)
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Run the whole exchange, \emph{hola} to \emph{adiós}, without stopping.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which goodbye for someone you won't see for a long time? (\emph{Adiós}.) Which everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}until\textquotedblright{} did Spanish take from Arabic? (\emph{hasta}.) You can now open \emph{and} close a conversation in Spanish. Next chapter: \textbf{por favor} and \textbf{gracias}' partner courtesies, then into everyday verbs.
\end{tcolorbox}
